messages.subject: breeding pairs and distance sampling
parts:
Dear listmembers,

I have a methodological question about point counts, breeding pairs and d=
istance sampling.=20
In The Netherlands our main method of monitoring birds is territory mappi=
ng. However, we are now developing a point count method for better covera=
ge (so far only for the agricultural areas, but it will probably be exten=
ded to include all habitats).=20
With territory mapping one counts breeding pairs, not individual birds. W=
e would like to do the same with point counts, as it is difficult to 'tra=
nsform' individuals into breeding pairs afterwards. This means that a sin=
ging male is considered to be part of a breeding pair, of which the femal=
e is not visible, and thus will count as a breeding unit, in the same way=
as an obvious pair would. We ask people to map all 'breeding units' with=
a simplified breeding code within 300m from a specified point (non-breed=
ing individuals are also mapped, but will be excluded from the analysis).=
Points are visited 4 times during the breeding season and species specif=
ic date-limits are set, so that only counts within the date limits (=3Dop=
timal breeding period) are used in the analyses.=20
In the literature I only find point counts counting individuals, not bree=
ding pairs, and nothing about date-limits.=20

I was wondering whether using breeding units instead of individuals will =
pose problems in analyses with Distance?
If so, can they be overcome (for instance by including breeding code as a=
covariate)?

Thank you,

Best regards,


Maja Roodbergen

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: breeding pairs and distance sampling
parts:
Maja, for songbird surveys of this type, we recommend that individuals
are recorded, but restrict this to singing males. See e.g.
Buckland, S.T. 2006.Point transect surveys for songbirds:robust
methodologies./The Auk/ *123*, 345-357.

Hopefully for most species, estimates of numbers or densities of singing
males will equate fairly closely with numbers or densities of breeding
pairs. As you note, females tend to be less detectable, and detection
at the point may not be certain, so that singing males satisfy the
assumptions of point transect sampling better than females do.

Steve Buckland

> > I have a methodological question about point counts, breeding pairs and distance sampling.
> > In The Netherlands our main method of monitoring birds is territory mapping. However, we are now developing a point count method for better coverage (so far only for the agricultural areas, but it will probably be extended to include all habitats).
> > With territory mapping one counts breeding pairs, not individual birds. We would like to do the same with point counts, as it is difficult to 'transform' individuals into breeding pairs afterwards. This means that a singing male is considered to be part of a breeding pair, of which the female is not visible, and thus will count as a breeding unit, in the same way as an obvious pair would. We ask people to map all 'breeding units' with a simplified breeding code within 300m from a specified point (non-breeding individuals are also mapped, but will be excluded from the analysis). Points are visited 4 times during the breeding season and species specific date-limits are set, so that only counts within the date limits (=optimal breeding period) are used in the analyses.
> > In the literature I only find point counts counting individuals, not breeding pairs, and nothing about date-limits.
> >
> > I was wondering whether using breeding units instead of individuals will pose problems in analyses with Distance?
> > If so, can they be overcome (for instance by including breeding code as a covariate)?

> >
> > Thank you,
> >
> > Best regards,
